## 2. Controls-to-ITIL Mapping with Required Evidence

This section maps your existing ITIL-aligned processes to the ISO 27001 controls they support, ranked by certification impact.

### Tier 1 — High value: existing processes that directly satisfy controls

**Incident Management (ITIL) → 5.24–5.28, 8.16**

Your ITIL incident process already covers detection, logging, categorization, escalation, and resolution. To satisfy ISO 27001 you need to add a security event classification scheme (e.g., P1-security: confirmed breach of PHI), security-specific playbooks (ransomware, data exfiltration, compromised credentials), a post-incident review template that feeds findings into the risk register, and evidence of forensic preservation where relevant.

Evidence the auditor will want: incident tickets showing security classification, playbook documents, post-incident review records with corrective actions, trend reports presented to management.

**Change Enablement (ITIL) → 8.32, 5.8**

Your change process is a strength. Add a mandatory security impact field on the change record (data classification affected, controls impacted), require CISO or security-team approval for changes touching production, PHI, or access controls, and link change records to vulnerability remediation (patching).

Evidence: change records with security-impact assessment, CAB minutes showing security sign-off, emergency change records with retrospective security review.

**Service Configuration Management / CMDB (ITIL) → 5.9, 8.9**

Extend the CMDB to include data assets and their classification, SaaS vendor inventory with data-flow mappings, cloud resources (IaC-sourced if possible), and ownership and custodianship fields.

Evidence: CMDB export showing asset owners and classification, reconciliation reports (drift detection), data-flow diagrams.

**Access Management (ITIL) → 5.15–5.18, 8.2, 8.3, 8.5**

Formalize the joiner/mover/leaver workflow with security controls: role-based access matrices per system, quarterly access reviews with sign-off, privileged access requests as auditable tickets, and MFA enforcement logs.

Evidence: access request tickets with approval chain, quarterly review spreadsheets signed by system owners, PAM session logs, MFA enrollment reports.

### Tier 2 — Medium value: processes to extend or formalize

**Problem Management (ITIL) → 5.27, 8.8**

Link problem records to vulnerability root causes. When a vulnerability is exploited or a near-miss occurs, open a problem record, perform root-cause analysis, and track the corrective action.

Evidence: problem records linked to security incidents, root-cause analysis documents, trend analysis.

**Service Continuity Management (ITIL) → 5.29, 5.30**

Document recovery time and recovery point objectives for the SaaS platform, integrate security scenarios (ransomware, cloud provider outage, insider attack) into BCP/DR plans, and test at least annually.

Evidence: BCP/DR plan with security scenarios, test reports with lessons learned, management sign-off on RTO/RPO.

Evidence: vendor risk register with risk ratings, contract extracts showing security clauses, annual vendor review records, SOC 2 reports on file.

# ISO 27001 Certification Roadmap — Continued

---

## 2. Controls-to-ITIL Mapping (Completed)

### Tier 2 — Continued

**Release and Deployment Management (ITIL) → 8.25, 8.26, 8.28, 8.29**

Embed security into your CI/CD pipeline: SAST scanning on every pull request with a policy that blocks merges on high/critical findings, dependency scanning (SCA) for third-party libraries on every build, DAST scanning against staging environments on a scheduled cadence (weekly or per release), container image scanning if you deploy containers to your IaaS environment, and a release gate that requires a security checklist sign-off before production deployment. Threat modelling should be performed for new features or significant architecture changes, documented as part of the design phase, and stored alongside the change record.

Evidence the auditor will want: CI/CD pipeline configuration showing security scan stages, scan result logs with remediation timelines, threat model documents linked to change or feature records, penetration test reports (at least annual, ideally after major releases), and secure coding standards document acknowledged by developers.

**Monitoring and Event Management (ITIL) → 8.15, 8.16, 5.7**

Centralize logs from cloud infrastructure, application layer, identity provider, endpoint agents, and network devices into a SIEM or managed detection platform. Define use cases and alert rules covering failed authentication spikes, privilege escalation, data exfiltration indicators, anomalous API usage, and changes to security configurations. Establish a triage workflow that routes security alerts into your incident management process with appropriate SLAs.

Evidence: SIEM deployment records and log-source inventory, alert rule documentation, triage runbooks, monthly detection metrics (alerts generated, investigated, escalated), log retention configuration showing at least 12 months.

**Service Request Management (ITIL) → 5.15, 5.18, 8.2**

Use your existing service request catalogue to create standardized, auditable request types for new user access, elevated or privileged access, firewall rule changes, and exception requests against security policy. Each request type should have a defined approval chain that includes security review for sensitive requests.

Evidence: service catalogue entries, completed request tickets with approval timestamps, exception request register with risk acceptance sign-off.

### Tier 3 — New processes to build (limited ITIL coverage)

**Risk Management → Clause 6.1.2, 5.7, 8.8**

This is the core of the ISMS and is not well covered by ITIL alone. Establish a formal risk assessment methodology (likelihood × impact, qualitative or semi-quantitative), build a risk register seeded from your gap analysis and threat intelligence, define risk acceptance criteria approved by leadership, and perform a full risk assessment at least annually and after significant changes. Vulnerability management should feed directly into this process: scan results generate risk entries, and patching SLAs are derived from risk ratings.

Evidence: risk assessment methodology document, risk register with owner, rating, treatment plan, and status for each risk, risk acceptance records signed by appropriate management level, management review minutes discussing the risk register.

**Internal Audit Programme → 9.2, 5.35**

Plan a full cycle of internal audits covering all ISMS clauses and applicable Annex A controls before the Stage 1 audit. You can use internal staff (trained and independent of the area being audited) or an external consultant. Produce an audit programme, individual audit plans, findings, and corrective action records.

Evidence: internal audit programme and schedule, audit reports with findings classified by severity, corrective action log with status and closure evidence, auditor competence records (training certificates).

**Management Review → 9.3**

Hold formal management reviews at planned intervals (quarterly is practical during implementation, then at least annually). Inputs include internal audit results, risk register status, incident trends, corrective actions, and changes in context. Outputs include decisions and resource commitments.

Evidence: management review meeting minutes with attendees, agenda items matching clause 9.3 inputs, documented decisions and action items.

**Document and Record Control → 7.5**

Establish a document control process covering version control, review and approval, distribution, and retention. This underpins every other control.

Evidence: document control procedure, document register with version history, evidence of review and approval (signatures or workflow records).

---

## 3. Prioritized 12-Month Project Plan

### Phase 0: Foundations (Months 1–2)

**Objective**: Secure commitment, define scope, and establish the ISMS framework.

Milestone 0.1 — Executive sponsorship and project launch (Week 2). Obtain board or executive committee approval, appoint an ISMS owner (likely your CISO or IT Director), allocate budget for tooling, training, consultancy, and certification body fees, and form a cross-functional ISMS steering group (IT, security, dev, HR, legal, operations). Deliverables: signed project charter, ISMS owner appointment letter, budget approval.

Milestone 0.2 — ISMS scope and context (Week 4). Document the scope (your healthcare SaaS platform, supporting infrastructure, hybrid cloud, on-prem, corporate IT, and third-party SaaS), identify interested parties and their requirements (customers, regulators, healthcare bodies), and document the internal and external context (Clause 4). Deliverables: scope statement, context of the organization document, interested parties register.

Milestone 0.3 — Risk methodology and initial gap assessment (Week 8). Define your risk assessment methodology and acceptance criteria, conduct the full gap analysis using the checklist in this document, and produce the initial risk register seeded from gap findings. Deliverables: risk assessment methodology, completed gap-analysis checklist, initial risk register with ~40–60 risks prioritized by severity.

### Phase 1: Core Policy and High-Priority Controls (Months 3–5)

**Objective**: Close the highest-risk gaps, build the policy framework, and start the vulnerability management overhaul.

Milestone 1.1 — Information security policy suite (Month 3). Write and approve the top-level information security policy plus supporting policies for access control, data classification, acceptable use, cryptography, supplier security, secure development, and incident response. Assign document owners and set review cycles. Deliverables: approved policy documents, document register.

Milestone 1.2 — Data classification and asset inventory (Month 3–4). Implement a classification scheme (Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted–PHI), extend the CMDB to cover data assets, cloud resources, and SaaS subscriptions, and produce data-flow diagrams showing where PHI is stored, processed, and transmitted. Deliverables: classification policy, updated CMDB, data-flow diagrams.

Milestone 1.3 — Vulnerability management programme (Month 3–5). Deploy or configure vulnerability scanning across infrastructure, cloud workloads, and applications, define scanning cadence (infrastructure weekly, application DAST weekly, dependency SCA on every build), establish remediation SLAs (critical: 72 hours, high: 7 days, medium: 30 days, low: 90 days), assign ownership for remediation tracking, and integrate scan findings into the risk register. Deliverables: vulnerability management policy and procedure, scanner deployment records, first scan reports, remediation tracking dashboard.

Milestone 1.4 — Privileged access and authentication hardening (Month 4–5). Implement PAM tooling for cloud admin, database, and production access, enforce MFA on all user and admin accounts across all systems, review and document role-based access matrices, and schedule first quarterly access review. Deliverables: PAM deployment records, MFA enforcement reports, RBAC matrices, access review schedule.

Milestone 1.5 — Secure development lifecycle (Month 4–5). Integrate SAST and SCA into CI/CD pipelines with blocking policies, document secure coding standards, train developers, establish a threat modelling process for new features, and schedule first annual penetration test. Deliverables: pipeline configuration evidence, secure coding standard, developer training records, threat model template, pen test contract.

### Phase 2: Extend Controls and Operationalize (Months 5–8)

**Objective**: Build out remaining controls, embed processes, and start generating evidence.

Milestone 2.1 — Supplier security programme (Month 5–6). Build the vendor risk register covering all third-party SaaS vendors, classify vendors by data access tier, collect current SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certificates, review and update contracts for security clauses and DPAs, and define an annual vendor review cycle. Deliverables: vendor risk register, contract amendment tracker, vendor evidence library.

Milestone 2.2 — Logging, monitoring, and detection (Month 5–7). Deploy or configure centralized logging with at least 12 months retention, implement SIEM or managed detection with use cases covering your top risks, integrate security alert triage into your ITIL incident process, and document monitoring procedures. Deliverables: log-source inventory, SIEM deployment records, alert rule documentation, triage runbook, first monthly detection metrics report.

Milestone 2.3 — Business continuity and DR (Month 6–7). Update BCP/DR plans to include security scenarios (ransomware, cloud provider failure, insider threat), validate RTO and RPO for the SaaS platform, and schedule a DR test. Deliverables: updated BCP/DR plan, DR test plan.

Milestone 2.4 — Security awareness and training (Month 6–7). Deploy a security awareness platform with healthcare-specific content (PHI handling, phishing, social engineering), run a baseline phishing simulation, establish quarterly training cadence, and ensure all staff complete initial training. Deliverables: training platform records, phishing simulation results, completion reports.

Milestone 2.5 — Remaining control implementation (Month 7–8). Close medium and low-priority gaps from the checklist: physical controls review, data masking in non-production, DLP for email and cloud storage, network segmentation review, information transfer procedures, and remote working security. Deliverables: control implementation evidence per item.

### Phase 3: Assurance and Readiness (Months 8–10)

**Objective**: Prove the ISMS works, refine, and prepare for audit.

Milestone 3.1 — Statement of Applicability finalized (Month 8). Complete the SoA using the template below, covering all 93 Annex A controls with justification for inclusion or exclusion and implementation status. Deliverables: approved SoA.

Milestone 3.2 — Full risk assessment review (Month 8). Re-assess the risk register with updated control status, document residual risk and risk treatment plans, and obtain management sign-off on risk acceptance. Deliverables: updated risk register, risk treatment plan, risk acceptance records.

Milestone 3.3 — Internal audit cycle (Month 8–10). Execute internal audits covering all ISMS clauses and all applicable Annex A controls, document findings and assign corrective actions, and track corrective actions to closure. Deliverables: internal audit programme, audit reports, corrective action log.

Milestone 3.4 — Management review (Month 10). Conduct a formal management review with all clause 9.3 inputs (audit results, risk status, incident trends, metrics, corrective actions, changes in context), and document decisions and resource commitments. Deliverables: management review minutes.

Milestone 3.5 — DR test execution (Month 9–10). Execute the DR test, document results and lessons learned, and feed findings into corrective actions. Deliverables: DR test report, corrective actions.

Milestone 3.6 — Penetration test (Month 9). Execute the annual penetration test, remediate critical and high findings before Stage 1, and document remediation evidence. Deliverables: pen test report, remediation records.

### Phase 4: Certification (Months 10–12)

**Objective**: Pass Stage 1 and Stage 2 audits.

Milestone 4.1 — Stage 1 audit (Month 10–11). The certification body reviews ISMS documentation: scope, policies, SoA, risk assessment, internal audit results, and management review minutes. They assess readiness for Stage 2 and may raise observations. Address any Stage 1 findings immediately. Deliverables: Stage 1 audit report, corrective actions for any findings.

Milestone 4.2 — Remediate Stage 1 findings (Month 11). Close any nonconformities or observations raised at Stage 1. Deliverables: evidence of corrective actions.

Milestone 4.3 — Stage 2 audit (Month 11–12). On-site (or hybrid) audit assessing implementation effectiveness. Auditors will interview staff, sample evidence, observe processes, and test controls. For a 350-person healthcare SaaS organization, expect 8–12 auditor-days. Deliverables: Stage 2 audit report, certificate (assuming no major nonconformities).

Milestone 4.4 — Post-certification actions (Month 12 and ongoing). Close any minor nonconformities from Stage 2 within the agreed timeframe, establish the surveillance audit schedule (typically every 6 or 12 months), and transition the ISMS into business-as-usual with continual improvement. Deliverables: corrective action closure, surveillance audit calendar, ISMS continual improvement plan.

Glad it's all in one place now. A few practical suggestions as you kick off:

**Engage your certification body early.** Contact an accredited CB in Month 1 or 2 and book a Stage 1 slot for around Month 10. Availability can be tight, especially for healthcare, and locking the date creates a firm deadline that keeps the project honest.

**Don't underestimate the documentation effort.** The policies, procedures, and risk register are where most teams lose time. Assign a dedicated ISMS coordinator — even part-time — to own document drafting, version control, and evidence collection. This person saves the CISO and control owners enormous time.

**Leverage what you already have.** Your ITIL-aligned incident, change, and CMDB processes are a real advantage. In many organizations those take months to build from scratch. Focus your energy on the genuine gaps — vulnerability management, supplier security, secure development, and monitoring — rather than rebuilding what works.

**Budget items people forget:** penetration testing (plan for two rounds if you want one before Stage 1 and one annual), security awareness platform licensing, PAM tooling, SIEM or MDR service, and the certification body fees themselves (Stage 1 plus Stage 2 for a 350-person scope can run $15,000–$30,000 depending on the CB and region).
